Introduction
A mangled extremity is a limb with injuries to at least three of the following systems: bone,
nerves, vessels, and soft tissue.1
This definition encompasses a wide variation in severity of injuries.
In civilians, mangled extremities typically result from high-energy blunt mechanisms of injury.
In the military, mangled extremities more often result from blast injuries.
Historically, amputations frequently were the end result; however, in the past few decades,
limb salvage has been shown to be a viable treatment option.
Each case is unique, and numerous factors must be considered in deciding between limb
salvage versus amputation.

Addressing airway, breathing, and circulation is the first priority in a patient with a mangled
extremity.
Early administration of antibiotic agents reduces infection.

Initial Management and Evaluation
In the treatment of a patient with a mangled extremity, Advanced Trauma Life Support
protocol must be followed. These patients typically are injured via a high-energy
mechanism; therefore, the airway, breathing, and circulation should be addressed
before the extremity. Although the mangled extremity often is a distractor, surgeons
must stabilize the patient and identify other injuries that may be life-threatening.
After resuscitation has been initiated, the limbs should be examined carefully. Open
fracture wounds and other large open wounds are inspected, and gross debris is
removed. A saline dressing should be placed, and the wound should be covered until the
patient undergoes débridement. A thorough vascular examination should be performed,
including palpating pulses and determining the ankle-brachial index. Palpable pulses and
an ankle-brachial index higher than 0.9 is associated with a 100% sensitivity in ruling out
vascular injury.2 Signs of an arterial injury include absent or asymmetric pulses, pulsatile
bleeding or expanding hematoma at the injury site, difference in skin temperature, or a
thrill or bruit. Vascular consultation should be obtained if a major vascular injury is
present. Any active bleeding should be controlled via a pressure dressing or a proximal
tourniquet. Skeletal stability of fractures and dislocations should be attained, potentially
including provisional or definitive fixation and providing a stable soft-tissue envelope
with restored length to support revascularization. If critical ischemia is present, then
vascular management should occur before orthopaedic management.3 Motor and
sensory examinations also should be performed. Gross alignment of the limb should be
restored, and splints or traction should be applied for provisional stabilization.
Antibiotic agents and tetanus prophylaxis should be administered on presentation in
patients in whom an open fracture is suspected. The timing of antibiotic agents is the
most important factor in reducing gram-positive and gram-negative infections.4 Lack et
al5 reported more infections after type III tibia fractures if antibiotic agents were

administered after a mean 66 minutes postinjury. Administration of a first- or second-
generation cephalosporin, such as cefazolin, is recommended for Gustilo-Anderson type
I or type II open fractures. The addition of an aminoglycoside is suggested for type III
open fractures. For open fractures with soil contamination or ischemia, penicillin also is
recommmended.6,7 The duration of antibiotic administration is controversial; however,
the cessation of antibiotic agents 24 hours after fixation recently has been
recommended.6
Suspicion for compartment syndrome should be high because it occurs in as many as
10% of patients with an open fracture.8 Compartment releases should be performed if
the differential pressure between the compartment and diastolic blood pressure is lower
than 30 mm Hg.9
Complete imaging studies of the injured extremity should be obtained, including
radiographs of the joints proximal and distal to the injured site.
Scores/Protocols
Scoring systems were developed to aid in decision-making regarding limb salvage versus
amputation.
No scoring system has been found to be accurate in predicting lower extremity amputation.10

Scores/Protocols
Deciding between limb salvage versus amputation is complex, and multiple factors
should be considered. Scoring systems and protocols have been proposed to guide the
decision-making process. In 1985, Lange et al11 reviewed type IIIC open tibia fractures to
determine whether an amputation should be performed on initial presentation.
Proposed absolute indications were complete tibial nerve disruption in an adult or a
crush injury with warm ischemia for more than 6 hours. Relative indications were serious
associated polytrauma, severe ipsilateral foot trauma, or a projected long course to
complete recovery. The authors suggested that if one absolute indication or at least two
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:38 PM
AAOS | Mangled Extremity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003017
3/18

relative indications were present, then amputation was indicated for the management of
type IIIC open tibia fractures. This did not include other mangled extremities with viable
vascularity.
The Mangled Extremity Severity Score was developed to help determine which lower
extremity injuries warrant primary amputation.12 The scoring system is based on
skeletal and soft-tissue injury, limb ischemia, shock, and patient age (Table 1). A score
greater than or equal to seven was proposed as indication for an amputation. Multiple
other scoring systems have been published, including the Predictive Salvage Index; the
Limb Salvage Index; the Nerve Injury, Ischemia, Soft Tissue Injury, Skeletal Injury Shock
and Age of Patient Score, and the Hannover Fracture Scale-97. Bosse et al10
prospectively studied these scores and the Mangled Extremity Severity Score to evaluate
their clinical utility in the Lower Extremity Assessment Project study. Low scores were
able to predict limb salvage potential (high specificity); however, higher scores were not
able to reliably predict the likelihood of amputation (low sensitivity). None of the scoring
systems were helpful in determining indications for amputation.

Surgical Management
In injured patients with a mangled extremity, the injury may be surgically débrided and
provisionally stabilized while determining whether limb salvage versus amputation is
preferable.
In critically ill, unstable patients with a mangled extremity, amputation may be lifesaving
because it promotes hemostasis and reduces the systemic burden of injury

Surgical Management
If a patient is adequately resuscitated, surgical débridement and stabilization (if
indicated) should be performed. Although the relationship between time to débridement
and infection risk in patients with an open fracture is a subject of debate,5,13-16 elective
delay of management is not recommended.14 A mangled extremity is not the same as
simple open fracture. A mangled extremity often includes severe soft-tissue damage,
bone loss, vascular compromise, and deep foreign body contamination and should be
débrided expeditiously in the operating room. A recent meta-analysis showed that high-
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:38 PM
AAOS | Mangled Extremity
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003017
5/18

grade open fractures with increased time to surgical débridement were associated with
an increased risk for infection.17
Primary amputation may be necessary. Few concrete indications exist for primary
amputation. Lange et al11 described absolute indications as a complete disruption of the
posterior tibial nerve in adults and crush injury with a warm ischemia time for longer
than 6 hours; however, initial plantar sensation is not predictive of long-term plantar
sensation or functional outcomes.18 If a decision is made to proceed with an
amputation, it should be performed at the most distal functional level possible. The level
at which to perform the amputation should be determined based on tissue viability; no
necrotic or devitalized tissue should be left behind. It is difficult to predict which limbs to
amputate and which limbs to salvage in borderline patients. A limb is not worth a life;
critically ill polytrauma patients with a type IIIC injury and hemodynamic instability
should undergo urgent amputation to save their lives. Conversely, borderline patients
(grade III injury) who are stable may undergo débridement, followed by splinting or
bridging via temporary external fixation and excisional débridement. This promotes
better understanding of the injury; allows for additional diagnostic testing; allows for
plastic surgery consultation; and most importantly, provides an opportunity to fully
discuss the details with the patient and/or his or her family. The patient can then make
an informed decision about limb salvage, which involves longer treatment timelines,
additional surgical procedures, and high initial costs.
If limb salvage is pursued, excisional débridement by an experienced trauma surgeon is
important.14,15 Devitalized tissues and bone are excised, and the wound is copiously
irrigated. The Fluid Lavage in Open Wounds trial, which included patients 18 years or
older who had an open fracture requiring fixation, concluded that low-pressure irrigation
was an acceptable alternative to high-pressure irrigation, with saline being superior to
castile soap solution.19 A sterile dressing or a negative-pressure dressing can be applied
after débridement; however, in some patients with massive exposed soft tissue, the
amount of initial hemorrhage after negative-pressure wound therapy may be life-
threatening, likely exacerbated by coagulopathy often present in such patients with
massive hemorrhage. Repeat surgical débridement every 24 to 72 hours, depending on
surgeon preference, should be performed until the wound is clear of devitalized tissue.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:38 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003017
6/18

Unstable fractures also should be stabilized during the initial visit to the operating room.
This should be achieved via provisional fixation with the use of a static external fixator.
Occasionally, injuries may be sufficiently supported with the use of an external splint.
Temporary external fixation may be advantageous because it is a fast method to
stabilize fractures with limited blood loss while minimizing foreign material in open
wounds. External fixator pins should be placed outside of the zone of injury but must be
as stable as possible to prevent gross movement in a non–weight-bearing patient
(Figure 1). Stability of bone and soft tissue has been shown to reduce infection,20 likely
by allowing host defense systems to react to bacteria contamination and prevent
additional tissue cell death.21 It also promotes subsequent radiography. The orthopaedic
surgeon should provide a stable frame that permits plastic surgery access for soft-tissue
coverage.
Figure 1 Illustrations of the lower leg show external fixation for damage-control surgery.
A, Anterior view illustration shows the zone of fracture, zone of soft-tissue injury, and
zone of definitive surgery. External fixation must be applied outside the zone of injury.
The zone of definitive surgery should be bridged, if possible. Anterior (B) and medial (C)
view illustrations show the application of external fixation.

7/18

Many options are available for definitive fixation, including open reduction and internal
fixation with the use of screws and plates, intramedullary fixation, and ring fixation. The
decision should be based on the fracture pattern, excessive soft-tissue dissection should
be avoided. Rozbruch et al22 described a technique to simultaneously manage bone and
soft-tissue defects via the Ilizarov method, which decreases the need for soft-tissue
coverage. Ilizarov limb reconstruction is cost-effective compared with amputation if the
cost of prostheses are included.23 An additional advantage of wire ring external fixation
is its utility in the management of infected nonunions.24
Depending on the level of soft-tissue damage and skin loss, primary wound closure may
not be possible, and management via split-thickness skin grafting or soft-tissue coverage
may be necessary. The orthopaedic surgeon must be creative and cooperative with the
plastic surgeon. Without a successful muscle flap, limb salvage often is not possible. The
timing of flap coverage is controversial. Lack et al5 reported that a delay to flap coverage
of more than 5 days in in patients with an type III open tibia fracture was associated with
deep infection and that a delay to flap coverage of more than 3 days in patients with a
type IIIB tibia fracture was most predictive of infection. Liu et al25 reported that patients
who underwent free-flap reconstruction for the management of severe open lower-limb
trauma within 3 days postinjury had lower rates of wound infection, flap revision
surgery, deep metal infection, and osteomyelitis compared with patients who underwent
free-flap reconstruction more 7 days postinjury. If free-flap reconstruction is performed
with a temporizing external fixator in place, definitive fixation, whether via plate, nail, or
ring fixation, should not be undertaken until approximately 6 weeks after muscle flap
reconstruction, if possible. This allows the flap to mature, allows soft-tissue swelling to
decrease, and reduces the risk for early infection.
Bone defects are common and can occur acutely after the débridement of devitalized
bone or in patients with an infected nonunion that develops later. Various treatment
options are available for the management of acute bone defects, including acute
grafting,26 the Masquelet technique,27 vascularized fibular grafting,28 Ilizarov
techniques,22,29 and acute shortening with or without later lengthening.30
Late or delayed amputation also is an option for patients who are initially treated via
limb salvage. The most common reasons for a late amputation are pain, poor residual

function, or chronic infection.31
Outcomes

Outcomes
Several studies have assessed the outcomes of patients who underwent treatment for a
mangled extremity. The Lower Extremity Assessment Project study included a
prospective cohort of 601 patients admitted to eight level I trauma centers.32 Failed limb
salvage was associated with increased costs and increased mortality. No difference in
functional outcome was observed between the amputation and limb salvage groups at a
follow-up of 2 years and 7 years.33 Poor outcomes were associated with older age,
female sex, non–White ethnicity, lower education, smoking, poor health before injury,
disability litigation, severe soft-tissue injury, crush foot, and infection.34 However, few
surgeons were proficient in wire ring external fixation, and bone transport techniques
were very limited. The technology in this area has advanced in the past 20 years. The
FIXIT study is a prospective, multicenter randomized trial that compared 1-year
outcomes after management of severe open tibial shaft fractures. Patients (254 total)
were randomized to modern external ring fixation or internal fixation (intramedullary
nail or plate).35 The results of this study revealed no difference between the internal and
external fixation groups with regard to infection; however, a significantly higher number
of major limb complications occurred in the external fixation group compared with the
internal fixation group (43.7% versus 64.6%; P = 0.002).36
In the Lower Extremity Assessment Project study, patients who underwent transtibial
amputation had a better performance on the timed test for walking speed than patients
who underwent transfemoral amputation. Patients who underwent through-knee
amputation had poorer Sickness Impact Profile scores and slower self-selected walking
speeds.37 Data suggest that performing a late amputation does not affect the mental
health of limb salvage patients postoperatively based on rates of depression,
posttraumatic stress disorder, and other mental conditions.31

Complications
Early and late complications are common in patients with a mangled extremity injury.
Bone transport with ring external fixation is an option for the management of nonunion with
extensive bone loss.

Complications
Complications are common after mangled extremity injury. Harris et al38 described
complications after mangled extremity injury (Table 2). Rehospitalization is the most
common complication, occurring in 48% of patients who undergo limb salvage and
29.8% of patients who undergo amputation. Infections also are very common. Harris et
al38 reported an 8.6% infection rate in patients who underwent limb salvage and zero
infections in patients who underwent amputation. Pollak et al15 reported a 27% infection
rate in patients who sustained open, high-energy lower extremity trauma. The authors
noted that the timing of first débridement and the timing of first débridement to
coverage were not predictive of infection; however, timely transfer to a level I trauma
center and time to first dose of antibiotic agents were associated with infection risk.

Bone transport with external ring fixation via stacked hexapod systems is an option for
the management of nonunion in patients with extensive bone loss.24,39 Prior implants
are removed, infected bone is resected, and antibiotic beads are placed on a suture
string at the defect site. Intraoperative cultures are obtained, and targeted systemic
antibiotic agents administered based on the culture results. A stacked ring hexapod
external fixator is applied, and a corticotomy is made away from the nonunion site. A
fibular osteotomy is necessary if angulation, translation, shortening, or rotation was
present at the nonunion site. Simultaneous shortening and lengthening programs are
commenced at similar rates. If the remaining defect is 1 to 2 cm in size, the antibiotic
beads are removed, and autologous iliac crest bone graft is placed at the docking site.
The program is continued until the docking site is compressed, and progressive weight
bearing is permitted during the consolidation period. The frame is then dynamized. In
some patients, adjunctive fixation with the use of a plate and screws or an
intramedullary nail may be necessary before frame removal. Adjunctive internal fixation
has not been associated with more infections, and it prevents loss of alignment.24,39 This
method40 (Figure 2) is associated with optimal long-term outcomes, potentially
approaching normal function.24
Figure 2 Illustrations of a tibia and fibula show bone transport and external ring fixation
with the use of stacked hexapod systems. IVATB = Intravenous antibiotic agents.
(Reproduced with permission from Sontich JK: Posttraumatic Taylor spatial frame
deformity correction in adults. Oper Tech Orthop 2011;21[2]:129-143.)


Case Presentation
The patient in this case presentation is a 29-year-old woman who sustained a right type
IIIB open tibial shaft fracture during a motorcycle collision. She was taken to the
operating room urgently for irrigation and débridement, the placement of a temporary
external fixator, and the application of a negative-pressure dressing to the soft-tissue
defect (Figure 3, A and B). The patient had 10 cm of bone loss. After a discussion, the
patient elected to proceed with limb salvage. The patient was transitioned to a more
stable temporary frame, and antibiotic beads were placed at the bony defect (Figure 3, C
and D). Definitive free-flap coverage was performed by a plastic surgeon (Figure 3, E
and F). After the soft tissue had healed (6 weeks), the frame was converted to a
transport frame, and a proximal corticotomy was performed (Figure 3, G and H). The
patient returned to the operating room 2 months after transport. During this procedure,
the flap was elevated, the antibiotic beads were removed, and iliac crest bone graft was
placed at the docking site (Figure 3, I). The transport was performed until the docking
site aligned and compressed. After completion of the transport (Figure 3, J and K), the
frame was removed (Figure 3, L and M); however, the docking site was not united. With
bone length restored and soft tissue healed, an intramedullary nail was placed, which
resulted in complete healing and stability (Figure 3, N and O).

Summary

Summary
The management of mangled extremities is complex. Despite advances, complications
are common, and long-term functional outcomes may be difficult to predict. Scoring
systems should only be used to supplement decision making. A team-based approach to
the extremity and setting reasonable patient expectations are important, keeping in
mind the patient’s baseline function and vocation and accounting for physical, mental,
and social risk factors. An experienced limb salvage reconstruction surgeon should be
included in the team if available. If the patient decides that amputation is a better
treatment option after being completely informed, then the surgeon should never
attempt to convince them otherwise. In the opinion of the authors of this lesson, the
Lange criteria of complete vascular disruption in an open tibia fracture with a warm
ischemia time of more than 6 hours are very relevant; these limbs should never be
salvaged.
